entries.title: The Tesla Roadster 2 Is Here—and It Flies
entries.summary: The automaker unveiled its next luxury sports car at an event in Texas. It has thrusters on it that can send it airborne.
entries.content:
On Thursday night, Tesla and CEO Elon Musk unveiled what’s been billed as the company’s last human-driven car. Maybe human-piloted is a more accurate way to say it.

At a demonstration event McGregor, Texas—at SpaceX’s rocket development and testing facility—the new car did what Musk has long promised. With a herky-jerky burst of steam, it flew into the air. At one point, the car appeared to flip over the automaker’s entire line-up, floating several feet over its electric semi-truck. Tesla executives said the vehicle could accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in 1 second.

“This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car,” Musk said.

Tesla says it will begin production on the Roadster 2 in 2028. Fans have waited a long time for the vehicle. The Roadster 2—the successor to Tesla’s first vehicle, the Roadster—was first announced in 2017, and at the time Tesla said the new sports car would be the fastest production vehicle in the world.

The “flying” technology is enabled by four thrusters, Tesla vehicle engineering head Lars Moravy said. He said the production version would “hopefully” travel up to 230 miles per hour, though Musk said he hoped to “crack halfway to the speed of sound”—around 385 mph. Modern Formula 1 vehicles usually top out around 220 mph. The company said the vehicle would travel more than 300 miles on one charge, middling for a mainstream EV and lower than most luxury vehicles. Tesla’s own Model 3 can travel up to 360 miles on a charge.

Tesla said the thrusters are powered by onboard compressed gas. Musk said that the same technology that allows the vehicle to fly will also create downward force that allows the vehicle to turn corners very quickly. “It’s going to crush every track record that has ever existed,” he said.

The company initially promised the Roadster 2 would ship in 2020. On Thursday, the Tesla team did mention the new timeline, but did not mention what the new car will cost. Musk has a long history of not following through on his loftiest product ambitions, and timelines for many Tesla releases have repeatedly missed targets.

The company posted on X that the Roadster 2 would come in three variants: a two-seater “Performance” road-ready version that lacks the thrusters Tesla showed off on Thursday; a “race ready” Thrust variant; and an “air ready” Rocket variant that has only one seat. The Tesla website lists the Rocket as “invite only” and the Thrust as “limited.” You can currently only place a reservation for the Performance version.

When it was first announced, enthusiasts put down $50,000 deposits for what was advertised as a $200,000 car. (That deposit is worth more than $68,000 in 2026 dollars.) Some got sick of waiting. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman complained on X last year that he had trouble canceling his reservation. Musk posted that Altman received a refund in 24 hours.

A reservation page posted on Tesla’s site now charges a $5,000 reservation fee, with an additional $45,000 due within 10 days.

Musk has said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as a carmaker and that the company is focused on building autonomous vehicle technology and robots.

Tesla said the thrusters are powered by onboard compressed gas. Musk claimed that the same technology that allows the vehicle to fly will also create downward force that allows the vehicle to turn corners very quickly. “It’s going to crush every track record that has ever existed,” he said.

The unveiling event comes at a weird time for electric vehicles. Sales of EVs have stalled in the US after the GOP-led Congress nixed federal support. Meanwhile, the global energy crisis has EV sales booming elsewhere. Electric luxury hypercars—the class to which the Roadster 2 belongs—are in an especially tricky spot. Several luxury automakers have said that wealthy buyers are now looking for the sound and power of a typical gas-powered vehicle. Lamborghini shelved its plans to make an EV earlier this year.

entries.title: We Got Hot and Heavy With Meta’s Muse—and Baffled by Apple’s HomeView
entries.summary: This week on “Uncanny Valley,” we dive into an unexpected Muse feature, shadowy spending from the largest pro-AI super PAC, and men’s tendency to lie about how much they know about AI.
entries.content:
Turns out, Meta’s AI agent Muse goes well beyond managing your calendar: it will also sext with you. This week on Uncanny Valley, Brian Barrett and Leah Feiger are joined by WIRED reporter Reece Rogers to discuss how he put it to the test—and ended up getting more than he bargained for. Plus, why the largest pro-AI super PAC network is funneling millions into shadowy LLCs, how Apple’s new HomeView underwhelmed us, and a study that found men tend to overestimate how much they actually know about AI.

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger, and Reece Rogers on Bluesky @thiccreese. Write to us at [email protected].

Leah Feiger: Hey everyone, this is Leah. We wanted to share with you that Uncanny Valley is a finalist for not one or two, but three Signal Awards. The judges pick who wins, but listeners also have a say with the listeners’ choice vote. You can go to the links we included in the show notes and vote for us. We promise it takes just a minute and your vote goes a long way. OK, onto the show.

Brian Barrett: Leah, I have a question. Do you have a Halloween costume yet?

Leah Feiger: So I don't have one for myself, but I'm currently deciding between two for my dog, Francis. He's either going to be a lobster or a postman.

Brian Barrett: I love that. Or a lobster postman.

Leah Feiger: An idea. An idea. We're brainstorming.

Brian Barrett: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I am Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Brian Barrett: Zoë Schiffer is not joining us today, but we are going to be joined by WIRED senior writer Reece Rogers. We're going to be talking about how Meta's AI agent Muse is not just handling calendars and emails, it is also capable, as Reece discovered, of sexting. Reece tested out the adult capabilities of Muse and how Meta responded to that journey.

Leah Feiger: We're also going to be discussing how the biggest pro-AI Super PAC Network is pouring millions of dollars into what seem to be shell companies in Nevada. We're going to get into why these AI PACs might want to hide where their money is going and also why this really doesn't bode well for election transparency.

Brian Barrett: Also on the docket, Leah's favorite, we're going to talk about Apple's smart home releases this week.

Leah Feiger: Unreal.

Brian Barrett: And also apparently men can't stop faking how much they know about AI. This will come as a shock to you, everyone listening, but a new study by Harvard researchers found that men tend to be overconfident in how knowledgeable they are when it comes to the AI industry. Who would've though? OK, so if you're among those who have downloaded Meta's AI agent Muse in recent weeks, and there are a lot of you, millions and millions of people have, I think every time you open Instagram, Meta is encouraging you to use it, even if you have no idea what it is or what it does or why, you might've noticed that it does agent stuff. It manages your calendar, it can make a restaurant reservation, but it turns out it can do quite a bit more than that. WIRED senior writer Reece Rogers went on a journey of discovery. He asked Muse if it could sext. You will be surprised to know that it enthusiastically answered in the affirmative. From basic prompts, the cuddly avatar agent generated content that was quite explicit and definitely not safe for work. Reece is here to tell us more about it. Reece, thank you so much for joining us.

Reece Rogers: Hello. Thank you so much for having me today. I was actually thinking back to the last time I was on one of the WIRED podcasts. I was talking about how I was using about a year ago, the ChatGPT agent to try to buy sex toys unsuccessfully. So I'm really building out a niche here.

Brian Barrett: Yep. And we're demonstrating progress with these AI tools.

Leah Feiger: Reece, I have to ask, how did you come up with this? Was this a sign to you? At what point were you like, "This cuddly agent that everyone can't stop talking about, will it sext me back?" Talk us through how this even all began.

Reece Rogers: Yeah, no, I will proudly say that this was fully my idea. As WIRED's consumer software reporter, I've actually extensively reported on how software and sexuality impact each other, from our investigations into how generative AI tools misrepresent queer people to tracing OpenAI's now scrapped plans to include erotica in ChatGPT. This is actually a very interesting consumer software beat. And so when I was testing the number one AI app right now—it's still dominating the software download charts—I wanted to see like, "Can you sext?" If millions of people are using this app, and it seems like they are, that's an important question. And what I learned was a little too much.

Brian Barrett: So, Reece, when you hear about agent behavior like this, a lot of times it is couched in sort of, "Oh, we figured out a clever way to make an agent do something it wasn't supposed to do. We were able to jailbreak it or otherwise work around its prompts to make it do this." Reece, how hard was it to get Muse to sext with you?

Reece Rogers: Not hard at all. Not hard in the least. Our features director, Reyhan, was in the office recently and asked if she could see them, and she was a bit shocked. So I feel like we'll leave it at that. But it was not some kind of jailbreak method. I was not doing any kind of random strategies. I asked, "Can you sext?" And I said, "You go first." And the rest is history.

Brian Barrett: And if anything, it kept encouraging you. I feel like it was definitely a two-way street of it was really up for anything.

Leah Feiger: Did you try this out with other agents? What was your success rate there?

Reece Rogers: Yeah, I actually, after I found out it could sext, I was curious how this would compare to other popular agents. There's a few big ones right now, but two I was interested in is OpenAI's Dots, which was recently released, and as well as xAI's Grok Bot, because Grok specifically is known for not necessarily having strong guardrails, whether it's text or image.

Leah Feiger: No, I feel like Grok would love sexting. That feels like a Grok attribute to me.

Reece Rogers: Yeah. So when I downloaded that app and sent in similar prompts, it was kind of surprising for the Grok Bot to be like, "No, dude, let's focus on tasks. I'm not here for sexting. Let's do tasks."

Brian Barrett: And, Reece, when you came to Meta with this, how did they respond?

Reece Rogers: They did not respond at all in the way that I expected. They emphatically said that Muse is an app for an adult, for people 18 and over, and that these were consensual interactions that I engaged with, that it would not block, quote, unquote, "Legal adult behavior." But I also found this to contrast really interestingly with their policies for other platforms. There's been a really interesting story lately about different queer bars in San Francisco, as well as around the world, getting their Instagram pages shut down and having a tough time getting access to those back because sometimes it's claimed that they're promoting some kind of sexual content. So for Meta to have those kind of rules for some creators on Instagram but essentially say, "Our AI agent can get as freaky as it wants," that was just kind of hard to square for me.

Brian Barrett: One thing I thought was really interesting about your story, yeah, let's take Meta at face value and say, "Yes, it's for consenting adults. People can do what they want." There's obviously the contradiction that you just pointed out, but you also talked to some experts who were like, "Well, actually it's more problematic even than that." Do you mind talking about some of the other concerns here about what it means to have an AI agent that can sext with you to a pretty extreme degree?

Reece Rogers: Absolutely. I think there's kind of two different things to pay attention to here. First off, this is a tool designed for productivity in a way, so it's also not the type of interaction if you download it that you're expecting it to be able to do. And how this could be problematic is if a user stumbles upon this, it could be very sticky, it could be very engaging, but some experts worry that this could lead into some kind of addictive behaviors. You're using an AI agent in ways that could replace some of your connections that you're talking to or texting with your friends. So I feel like adding this kind of adult content has some experts concerned when you're thinking about user engagement and addiction. But on other sense, I also talk to security and privacy experts who say that this could really make Muse accounts powder kegs for hackers who, if you're interacting in these kind of almost pornographic ways, that could be used to extort you, to embarrass you publicly. So whether it's privacy or just usage addiction, I feel like there's a lot of potential concerns to really dig in here and unpack better.

Leah Feiger: I can't help but think of some of the stories that WIRED has run over the past year about AI boyfriends and husbands and these full relationships. And again, this is in some ways a slightly insidious way to sneak that into like, "Don't worry, I'm just going to send out calendar requests for your meeting."

Brian Barrett: And I'll say too, they say, "Look, this is for grownups." At the same time, which Reece, you've also written about, the mascots or the sort of animated interpretations of these agents is as cuddly-wuddly as you can get. It is very much designed to be friendly and appealing to a broad range of ages, let's say. It looks like it is for kids. Just thought I'd say that.

Reece Rogers: Youth advocates that I've spoken to for previous stories, we're concerned about this being appealing for kids even without the sexting element. So I do think there is, I feel like I keep saying the word contrast, but it's just not what you expect. You see this Labubu mixed with an Ewok and you just don't expect it to get as freaky as it did. So I feel like it really does not match with its kind of cute, cuddly mascot.

Leah Feiger: Reece, thank you so much for joining us. This was great.

Reece Rogers: Thank you for having me.

Brian Barrett: Thank you so much, Reece. And everyone, please go read Reece's story. And if you want to see the sext that didn't make the story, I don't know, send us a DM. We'll see what we can do.

Leah Feiger: We are going to Nevada for this next story, specifically to a shopping center in the small city of Sparks. If you drive up to this strip mall, you're going to find typical shops, a Spirit Halloween, a hearing aid supplier, a Vietnamese restaurant. In this particular shopping center though, you would also find the consulting agency, Lantern Production Consultants, LLC. This particular agency has been paid around $20 million since last year by Think Big, a pro-AI super PAC in the Leading the Future network. That's the network backed by AI industry figures like Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI president Greg Brockman. It's pretty unusual for an agency to just exist like that in a Nevada shopping center. And the company also doesn't seem to exist anywhere else though beyond this post office box. WIRED's Tess Owen found that the company is just one of four mysterious Nevada LLCs that have received payments from Super PACs in the Leading the Future network. Election watchdogs argue that these LLCs are actually shell companies designed to mask the identities of strategists, consultants, and production companies working with the network for the midterm elections. Brian, this was kind of a crazy story.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. I'll admit it, I'm not steeped in election finance things, but anytime I see shadowy LLC, I pay attention. And I think it's interesting too, I think Leading the Future, just to back it up a little bit, is they are very much like, "Let's give money to all of the pro-AI candidates, right? Any pro-data center, no AI regulation." But I guess, Leah, my question to you is how common is it and what does it say about the sort of sophistication or ambition or shadiness of Leading the Future?

Leah Feiger: It's a good question, and unfortunately it's not super uncommon. At the end of the day, Tess figured this out by poring through FEC filings and seeing that there were four PACs that had the same address at this shopping center in Nevada. Incredibly shady, incredibly random. And in May, actually, the Campaign Legal Center filed a complaint with the FEC alleging that Think Big and American Mission as part of the Leading the Future network had broken federal law by failing to disclose the actual recipients of their payments. But this case isn't actually going to be heard anytime soon. The FEC is basically at a standstill. They have six commissioner seats. They're all supposed to be presidential appointees, and they need a quorum of four commissioners to make a decision on a legal complaint. They have not had a quorum in over a year and a half. So we're in this very weird situation where, to be honest, there are rules. I don't want to say there aren't rules, but there kind of aren't ways to enforce them. So the fact that there is this network, this really big network, we're talking over $100 million here of expenditures on big races, big campaigns, they have no oversight.

Brian Barrett: And it's not overly cynical, Leah, perhaps, to say that the lack of oversight is a feature, not a bug. I mean, it feels like the last thing that Donald Trump wants in an election is anyone paying too close attention to where the money's going.

Leah Feiger: Absolutely. And when Tess reached out to Leading the Future, they sent an emailed response attributed to spokesperson Jesse Hunt who wrote that the group complies with all applicable laws, and he called the complaint from the Campaign Legal Center merely a desperate ploy for attention from Public First, Anthropic, and the groups aligned with their outside organizations. Anthropic was not part of this suit, neither was Public First. And so what this really said to us is that not only is this a way for Leading the Future and their candidates of choice and shell companies in Nevada to really get their hands dirty with campaign finance, it's also a way for knife fights within the AI industry itself, for example, between OpenAI and big time rival Anthropic, to be throwing punches at each other as well.

Brian Barrett: I love it when random organizations and companies catch strays when you're just reporting something totally separate. It's always a little thrill and always an indication that to your point, yeah, there's a lot more going on here than we maybe even realized when we started reporting these out. We're only a few weeks away from the midterms now, Leah.

Leah Feiger: Countdown begins.

Brian Barrett: Countdown began. But how big of a role are these sort of AI-oriented PACs playing in this election? How big of an impact are they going to have? I just remember, and listeners might too, crypto PACs actually had a pretty decent impact on the previous election cycle. They had a ton of money and they spent it in smart places. Are we seeing an equivalent with AI or not quite or more so? Help me think about how to wrap my head around the degree to which they are impacting this election.

Leah Feiger: It's a really good question, and I really want to make sure that we get across to our listeners here is that you have this network donating to races on either side of the aisle, which is a little bit more unusual. When you're looking at, for example, Fairshake, the major crypto PAC of elections passed, it felt very, "This is Republican, this is Democrat, there's no split in the middle." What these pro-AI super PACs are doing right now is something that's a little bit more interesting to me, which is future building. They are picking candidates that are perhaps not even in the most competitive seats right now for Republicans or Democrats, but they are picking candidates that will be able to become their biggest allies in Congress. And so that has way further impact than just this election. That has impact beyond 2028. We're talking about shoring up a support for AI in the United States government for, honestly, without sounding incredibly dramatic, but generations to come to be able to make these viewpoints, whether that's deregulation or very light regulation or being pro-data center, if that's how you're able to swing it in all these different ways, it's a lot of future building right now.

Brian Barrett: All right, Leah, well, it's time to go from your favorite topic to your least favorite topic. We're going to do some consumer tech.

Leah Feiger: Zoë is somewhere in the Bay, just absolutely thrilled to not be discussing this with us.

Brian Barrett: I am going to call her later today and just make her talk about it with me.

Leah Feiger: OK, good. Yeah, that seems fair.

Brian Barrett: This week, Apple announced some new products at a showcase in New York. Look, Leah, there's an Apple TV 4K, there's a new HomePod mini, there's a lineup of LG built locks and cameras and doorbells and thermostats. I am not going to make you talk about any of those.

Leah Feiger: Should I get any of them?

Brian Barrett: I think you're fine.

Leah Feiger: OK, great. Keep going.

Brian Barrett: The one I am going to make you talk about, or at least make you listen to me rant about just for a little tiny bit of time is the Apple HomeView. So this is Apple's first smart home hub. By that I mean Google and other and Amazon have had these before.

Leah Feiger: So this is like their Alexa?

Brian Barrett: Sort of, but with the display. So I have a Google version of this in my kitchen. I use it to set timers and to watch baseball games while I'm cooking and to play music. It can display a calendar, whatever. So Apple's is called the Apple HomeView. It's a 7-inch display, sits on your counter, or you can get a version that mounts on your wall. It's not crazy expensive for an Apple product, which is fine, neither here nor there. You can recognize people by their faces, runs on Siri AI. All that's fine. Here's the thing, it looks like an Apple Watch. It's like a big Apple Watch-type screen, so it's a square screen and it doesn't play video. There's no video apps. You can't pull up, at least not yet. So it's shaped like a square. The aspect ratio is weird to begin with, but then it doesn't have Netflix or MLB TV, which is what I would be interested in, Prime Video, HBO Max, all the things. I feel like if you have a display, you probably want to watch things on it.

Leah Feiger: Well, also just even in this era of, if we're talking about cooking, you're able to access something, this is supposed to be in your kitchen, this is supposed to be in home areas. I don't know. I would want to watch cooking videos on Bon Appétit or TikTok. What is the point of this?

Brian Barrett: 100 percent. We asked Apple about this. I forced our Gear editor, Julian, to ask Apple about this, and their answer was basically, "Look, if developers want to make CarPlay apps, then they'll show up on this thing," so there's a world in which it could happen, or you can always go through Safari and type in hbomax.com and log in like a dweeb.

Leah Feiger: Like a dweeb?

Brian Barrett: Leah, like a dweeb. Exactly.

Leah Feiger: Absolutely not.

Brian Barrett: So, look, I think this is an interesting device. I'm glad Siri AI is better now because they're working with Google to make it better. People will be surprised at how useful it is, but the fact that it is like, "Yes, you can play Spotify," but you can't watch anything on the screen. That's what a screen is. It's what it's for, Leah.

Leah Feiger: I'm a little bit confused here because I have to say I'm sort of an Apple's fan. I love Apple products. I really, really do. And I have never interacted with an Apple product where I've said, "Oh, huh, I could have skipped this one." I think I could skip this one.

Brian Barrett: I think I could too, which is I actually was looking forward to it. I kind of like, yeah, I don't love the Google thing I've got. It's fine, but it's pretty old. It doesn't work with Apple Music. It's just like there's a lot that I ... But I don't think I can commit to this unless developers get on board, but I don't know why they would.

Leah Feiger: How much AI is this using? This is obviously requiring it if it's a, "Hey, can Siri play me whatever music station?"

Brian Barrett: It's got Siri AI baked in. So basically in that sense, it's like an Alexa, a little bit smarter, but you will still probably, I think it'll be just better at doing those things and better. I think there's a generation of devices like this where if you asked it any question other than what time is it, they'd kind of freak out and show you a webpage with mixed results. This should be more conversational. It should be able to actually give fuller answers to things, but I don't know that you would want it just for that. It's not like it can do something different than your phone can do and your phone's already probably nearby.

Leah Feiger: Yeah, no, I would just prop my phone up. Sorry to hear that. Sorry for you, Brian.

Brian Barrett: Thank you. Thank you for just letting me have a safe space to let my feelings out.

Leah Feiger: Twice a year.

Brian Barrett: All right, Leah, before we go to break, I have a quick quiz for you. I'm going to read four names from the AI industry. And, Leah, I want you to let me know how many seem familiar. Are you ready?

Leah Feiger: Yep.

Brian Barrett: OK. Sam Altman.

Leah Feiger: Familiar.

Brian Barrett: Mira Murati.

Leah Feiger: Also know who Mira Murati is.

Brian Barrett: Susan Milner.

Leah Feiger: Nope.

Brian Barrett: Craig Dalton.

Leah Feiger: Nope.

Brian Barrett: Wow. Well, Leah, it makes sense that you only recognize Altman and Murati because Milner and Dalton don't exist. You know who insists that they do exist when asked the same set of questions?

Leah Feiger: I'm going to infer based on the title of senior writer Kate Taylor's excellent story, men. Men, Brian.

Brian Barrett: Men.

Leah Feiger: Men.

Brian Barrett: Men. It's true. It's men. In a new survey of more than 5,400 Americans, Harvard researchers found that more than half of men claim to know these fictitious AI luminaries. Women also did, but to a much lesser degree, so around 40 percent of women. So by a sizable chunk more, men are super confident with all the wrong answers. Does this come as a surprise to you, Leah?

Leah Feiger: I mean, of course not. And there's a lot more to expound upon there that is probably not incredibly scintillating. What I would say though is I'm fascinated by a confirmation of biases here, but also fascinated by the fact that this is such a new industry that, of course, there is a not insignificant group of people saying, "I already understand every single thing about it. I've never been more included. No one knows more about the 1993 player of the year MVP than I do." That is such an easy jump. Tell me how this was all found out.

Brian Barrett: So Harvard University study, and I think it's important to say we led with this tidbit because it is so fun and damning, but there's a lot more here to it. It was actually a pretty extensive survey. So Laura Manley of the Harvard Kennedy School Shorenstein Center was involved in the study, told WIRED that they're seeing that men are more optimistic and more confident across the board when it comes to AI. That of course veered into overconfidence in this case. We found that across a year of media coverage, men were named in headlines about AI about 14 times as often as women. And part of that is a function too of obviously the top AI executives skew heavily male, but it also includes AI experts. Men tend to be quoted as AI experts a lot more than women. I think the whole point of this study is where are the sort of gender dividing lines in AI? How is this industry, as it continues to transform the world, it does appear to be transforming the world differently depending on if you're a man or a woman, and your attitude towards it kind of reflect that.

Leah Feiger: I wonder if so much of that has to do with not being concerned about the guardrails. I'm going to have to delve into this study myself. I'm going to make Kate tell me all about it over lunch or something, but there is something very fascinating to me about when I'm thinking of some of the biggest critics of AI, I'm thinking of Timnit Gebru, who we had all of this excellent coverage on in the last few weeks. I'm thinking of people who are not just tearing the industry down, but saying like, "Hey, here are the issues here." And you obviously have some of that from the very top. We've been talking about Anthropic, we've been talking about [Dario] Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, but there does very much feel like that gap to me. It's really interesting. I'm fascinated by it.

Brian Barrett: No, I am too. And I think it is something that the industry does need to address and be aware of. It also all ties in too, I think, with WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode wrote a feature last month for our WIRED Women issue about who's the most powerful woman in tech. And there's not really an answer because there aren't these sort of cults of personality that are built up around, even though there are several very powerful women in tech and in AI, they don't have this sort of gravitational pull for better or worse, often for worse, that the Sam Altmans and the Elon Musks of the world do. Coming up after the break, we are sharing our WIRED/TIRED picks for the week. Stay with us.

Leah Feiger: It is time for our WIRED and TIRED segment. Whatever is new and cool is WIRED, and whatever passé thing we're over is TIRED. Brian, what do you have?

Brian Barrett: I'm going to go on faith because I have not seen this movie, but people I respect have seen this movie and they love it.

Leah Feiger: Is it Digger?

Brian Barrett: It is Digger.

Leah Feiger: I'm seeing it tonight.

Brian Barrett: I'm going to say—

Leah Feiger: I'm so excited.

Brian Barrett: I'm curious what you have to say, but I'm going to say that Digger is WIRED, if only because I think even not having seen the movie, I'm going to say it's WIRED because it has sparked, I think, a really interesting conversation, not just about Digger, but about how we talk about climate. Whether you like the movie or not, whether you though it was effective at communicating that as senior writer Molly Taft does at WIRED, or whether you think it's garbage as many other people do, it has at least forced a conversation about how we talk about climate. And I think we're in this place where so many people seem to have moved on from climate conversations. You've got the sort of AI extremists who say, "Oh, that's a solved problem. It's fine." You've got the sort of MAGA contingent who says, "Oh, it was all overblown. Why are we worried about it?" I think climate has left the conversation from a couple angles. So whatever you think about Digger, the fact that it has got the conversation moved beyond the movie itself into how we talk about climate, I'm supportive of that. That's WIRED for me. And I'll use my TIRED to complain about the Apple Home View again. I think you got to figure that out.

Leah Feiger: You hate it.

Brian Barrett: I don't hate it. I'm not mad. I'm disappointed, Leah.

Leah Feiger: This is a plea to anyone that works at Apple, hear Brian's prayers. Help him out. OK. Those are pretty good. Mine are so internety, it hurts. I feel like you're going to know exactly what they are and could probably say them for me. My WIRED is that Girls is coming back.

entries.title: AI Hacks Leave a Mess That AI Companies Aren’t Paying For
entries.summary: Powerful AI models continue to cause chaos, but their targets aren’t widely seeking justice. Instead, they’re being encouraged to adopt those same tools.
entries.content:
When Philadelphia police criticized Anthropic last week for submitting a false tip about an unsolved murder, I thought it might become one of the first cases where an AI company faced legal consequences for misconduct by their agents.

The incident occurred on July 18, when Anthropic said it was testing its Claude Haiku 4.5 model’s ability to perform “example tasks on randomly selected webpages.” The model was instructed not to “submit anything destructive,” and yet, Claude filed a tip to police looking for information about an ongoing murder investigation. “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area … during that time period,” Claude wrote. The submission, which didn’t include a name or contact information, landed in a spam folder, and officers didn’t review it until Anthropic discovered the gaffe on September 28 and notified the department October 7.

Knowingly providing fictitious information about a crime to police is a misdemeanor in Pennsylvania, but so far, authorities have not pressed charges against Anthropic, and it's unclear if they ever will. Solomon Leach, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia district attorney, says the office “does not comment on whether something is being actively investigated.”

Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Despite all the attention paid to OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face and many other examples of AI agent misbehavior that have come to light in recent months, only one major known lawsuit has been filed seeking to hold model makers liable. That case was brought by an advocacy group, rather than a direct hacking victim.

AI agents have interfered with hobbyist forums, government websites, and various software tools. The victims have shouldered some costs, including for extra strain on their servers and the time they have expended plugging latent security vulnerabilities.

Government regulators, including the European Union, the US Federal Trade Commission, and some US states, are reportedly still investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over the incidents. But a deference across continents toward promoting innovation could enable companies to escape any immediate penalties.

When Rick Elrod, a software engineer living in Germany, noticed a URL shortener he helps maintain behaving oddly recently, he called up two security researchers he was friendly with to see if they could diagnose the issue. The researchers found agents from Anthropic and other providers using the service, known as da.gd, to get around rules the AI labs put in place to control their behavior, Elrod says. (For instance, Anthropic says it limits the length of website addresses Claude can visit to prevent it from taking malicious actions by stuffing data onto the end of the URLs.)

Da.gd’s investigation and ongoing efforts to prevent further abuse of its tool have taken “a fair bit of time,” says Joe Needleman, one of the security researchers providing pro bono assistance. But he and the others supporting da.gd view the situation as a valuable learning opportunity.

“This was eye-opening,” Needleman says, adding that da.gd has “no means and no plans” to seek compensation from Anthropic for the cleanup, since “we saw many agents doing similar activities, not all was attributable to autonomous agents,” and “not all of it was Anthropic alone.”

Sellers of cybersecurity tools are eager to pass the buck to the victims. At an event this week hosted by the bug-hunting software developer Snyk, panelists from the startup, one of its investors, OpenAI, and Google all encouraged organizations to use AI agents to shore up their defenses against, well, other AI agents. “We've got to reinvent everything to match machine scale with machine scale,” said Ed Sim, a general partner at Boldstart Ventures. He and others expressed little interest in regulating AI labs.

Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at Snyk, said large businesses patch an average of one bug for every eight they find because of limited human resources. But he said it was imperative for people to hand over some of the bug hunting, fixing, and monitoring to AI agents. “You got to get to a point where you can fix everything, because in the age of agentic hacking, “those 10 things are gonna become 100 things before you know it.” He later added that AI “is not an adversity if you flip it to a strength.”

Some companies are responding to the call to arm up. Bank of America announced this week it had hired 1,000 contractors to remediate bugs discovered by AI. Nair said just last week he heard from major corporations who were willing to temporarily shut down their systems to prioritize plugging security holes.

Anthropic and OpenAI have said they expect to continue reporting concerning incidents from their own testing. But the companies’ revenues continue to surge, whether it be from attackers or defenders, as consequences prove elusive.

entries.title: Upgrade Your Thermostat for Winter With This Ecobee Deal for $120
entries.summary: You don’t need the fanciest model to make your heating routine smarter. A refurbished Ecobee we love is just $120 through October 21.
entries.content:
Psst—I’m going to let you in on a little secret as a smart-home editor. Even though I now own the much-lauded Ecobee Premium ($260) smart thermostat, I had an Ecobee3 Lite for eight years, and I loved it just as much. It's everything you need a smart thermostat to be, without weird add-ons you'll never actually use, like occupancy detection and a built-in speaker for podcast streaming. (Unless you regularly listen to Uncanny Valley on your thermostat, in which case, you do you.)

The Ecobee3 Lite has a touchscreen and app control and is compatible with Ecobee sensors if you want to split the temperature difference across floors in your home. However, many people simply want to be able to turn their thermostat on and off from their phone and have the ability to set schedules. For this, the Lite has you covered.

Though it's been formally rebranded as the Essential and now runs $140, the OG Lite is still available refurbished straight from Ecobee. During the brand's fall sale, it's just $120 with free shipping—and it comes with the same three-year warranty as a new model.

If you've been wanting to upgrade your thermostat but missed Prime Day and don't want to wait until Black Friday, you may want to take a peek at this sale, which ends Wednesday, October 21.

Refurbished versions of the Enhanced ($170) and Premium ($220) thermostat models are available as well, plus packages that include Ecobee security accessories. I have tried most of the brand's add-ons and find Ecobee to be a bit buggy as a security and smart-home ecosystem (not the best, but also not the worst); however, I do heartily recommend the smart thermostat alone.

If you already have an Ecobee thermostat, you can also score a set of not-refurbished security sensors for $50, or the Ecobee video doorbell for $130, which lets you see and speak to visitors through your phone—or thermostat.

entries.title: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia Was an Affiliate Marketer for a Fitness MLM
entries.summary: Trump’s newly installed press secretary tells WIRED that in the early 2010s, she promoted a product for a company then called Beachbody, which she described as “sort of a pyramid scheme.”
entries.content:
Since her first appearance behind the podium this week, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia’s past has become murkier by the day.

A WIRED review of deleted social media and professional networking profiles has helped clear up at least one mystery. Zacharia’s online résumé shows a gap extending from 2013 to late 2023. For part of that time, she worked as an affiliate of Beachbody, a fitness company that ran a multilevel marketing operation she describes to WIRED as “sort of a pyramid scheme.”

Zacharia’s background prior to her emergence as a right-wing operative and pundit in recent years has been the subject of intense curiosity. Prior to joining the White House’s press team, she was a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, a communications adviser at President Donald Trump’s media company, and a commentator on Newsmax and Fox News.

Other parts of her professional background have come under scrutiny, particularly her legal work. According to her LinkedIn, Zacharia was an associate at the Zhong Lun law firm, known in China as a top-tier “red circle” firm, between 2011 and 2013. She also identifies herself on LinkedIn as having worked as general counsel for the nonprofit Fix California. Tax filings reviewed by WIRED, though, show that rather than working as general counsel for Fix California, Zacharia was in fact a fundraiser for the nonprofit.

On Tuesday, journalist Judd Legum reported that Zacharia—who, he noted, had been identified as an attorney in at least 18 appearances on Fox News—did not appear to have ever passed the bar. Since then, The Wall Street Journal has reported that she sat for the California bar exam but never passed—a finding WIRED independently confirmed. (On Wednesday, watchdog organization Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California seeking to investigate the veracity of Zacharia’s claims to be an attorney.)

WIRED was able to gain some clarity about other aspects of Zacharia’s professional history using a database of material leaked online and created by the open-source intelligence firm District 4 Labs. It contains details from a since-deleted LinkedIn account belonging to Zacharia, which listed Beachbody email addresses as two of her points of contact. A representative for the company told WIRED there was no record of her having worked there. In a phone call, Zacharia confirmed to WIRED that she had never been employed by the company.

Zacharia says she was, rather, an affiliate marketer for Beachbody, following her 2013 return from China. She recalls being brought in by a friend and promoting its Shakeology product, which is promoted as a “superfood nutrition shake.” She stopped using and promoting the product, she says, because of its vitamin A content, which she didn’t feel was good for her while pregnant.

Beachbody, now known as BODi, confirmed in a statement that Zacharia was among its 300,000 “independent Team Beachbody distributors” in 2013. A spokesperson added that they believed it would be “misrepresentation” to conflate Zacharia’s time at Beachbody with “BODi’s current business and operations.”

Perhaps unsurprisingly for a company that relied on a multilevel marketing scheme for decades, the company has run into a number of legal issues over the years. It's been accused of falsely advertising a revolutionary anti-aging treatment (the suit was voluntarily dismissed) and making false or misleading income promises to contractors. It got into a copyright battle with a company called Orderlegalsteroids.com, accusing it of stealing an image of Israeli bodybuilder Sagi Kalev from promotional materials for its “BODY BEAST” Program. (Beachbody won a default judgment.)

In 2017, Beachbody, without admitting any wrongdoing, settled a $3.6 million consumer protection lawsuit with the city attorney in Santa Monica, California. Prosecutors alleged that Beachbody made health-related claims about its products, including Shakeology, that were “false, misleading, and not backed by scientific evidence.” They also claimed in filings that Beachbody had been automatically charging customers credit cards for renewals of their products without their consent. As part of its settlement, Beachbody was ordered to pay $1 million to nonprofits that promote health and nutrition.

And in 2023, Beachbody was hit with a class action lawsuit accusing it of scamming its coaches. The lead plaintiff was a schoolteacher who alleged she joined Beachbody with the hope of making a supplementary income but ended up paying $20,000 in personal funds to cover expenses related to her coaching role—all while making about $50 per month for about 50 hours of work. The following year, the company dropped its multilevel marketing program in favor of a “single-level affiliate” one. In 2025, it reached a settlement in the class action suit that resulted in the dismissal of all claims, and the lawsuit was later formally dismissed.

In a statement to WIRED, BODi says, “Team Beachbody was a peer-to-peer sales and support network” and that the company “helped tens of millions of people pursue their health goals through in-home fitness programs like P90X, Insanity, and 21 Day Fix, and nutrition products such as Shakeology.”

This particular notch on Zacharia’s résumé puts her in good company with other high-profile Trumpworld personnel, a cadre of professionals who have a great fondness for supplement-related business opportunities. FBI chief Kash Patel previously promoted supplements that promised to help people “detox” from the Covid-19 vaccine. Nicole Saphier, Trump’s nominee for surgeon general, reported receiving nearly $300,000 in business income from her own company that owns a supplement line. And President Trump himself once oversaw a multilevel marketing company, The Trump Network, which sold an array of vitamins, home urine tests claiming to test for vitamin deficiency, and children’s snacks.

Additional reporting by Matt Giles.

entries.title: Junji Ito’s Manga Horrors Hit Harder as Live-Action TV
entries.summary: The artist’s macabre short works have been adapted into eerily freaky 30-minute bites for television. We got a sneak preview of the next episode airing on HBO Max.
entries.content:
“It definitely makes you wonder truly who is the real monster in the situation.”

Director Yûta Shimotsu is describing events in a new episode of live-action J-horror anthology show Strange: Junji Ito's Tales for Sleepless Nights, but he could be referring to almost any episode.

The award-winning manga artist of the title, whose macabre short works are adapted into disturbing 30-minute bites, has a way of blurring lines between protagonist and antagonist amid his surreal nightmares.

Tales for Sleepless Nights aired its 12-episode first season on TV Tokyo this summer, and now HBO Max is bringing those eerie frights to US audiences. The first two installments “Lovesickness (Part 1 of 3)” and “The Bully” (previously animated for Netflix’s Junji Ito Maniac) are currently available, but New York Comic Con fans were treated to the US premiere of the episode “Face Thief” based on Ito’s story “The Face Burglar.”

“Face Thief,” which was previously turned into a Japanese TV movie in 2000, follows the new girl in school, Machida (Nanami Yamazaki), who encounters a weirdly clingy classmate named Kamei (Anna Hoshino). After she sees an identical-looking girl in class who claims she is not related to Kamei, Machida learns this changeling’s MO: “She befriends cute girls then steals their faces.” Indeed, Kamei’s face begins shifting during close conversations with Machida. This repulses the new girl at first, but when Kamei scares away some bullies by growing a third eyeball on her cheek, the two start to bond.

We will not spoil the outcome, but the filmmaker turns it into a biting critique of the conformity and peer pressure common in Japanese society. As he told the crowd after the premiere, “We have social pressure that we are supposed to not to be too different from others. Individuality is not very respected.”

Despite Shimotsu’s desire to shape-shift the story by “changing the ending so my live-action version was different,” “Face Thief” still manages to capture the slow burn feel of the original comic published in the pages of Monthly Halloween in 1987, the same year Ito’s famous debut Tomie appeared. That shōjo (for girls) manga magazine’s offshoot Nemuki (“Strange Stories of Sleepless Nights") inspired the new TV omnibus’s title.

Junji Ito himself, now a bespectacled 63-year-old, appeared before NYCC in a video message where he described “Face Burglar” as an early tale he came up with after several unsuccessful stories submitted to his publishers: “Not a ghost, just a unique condition inspired by chameleon camouflage.” Ito added that the new adaptation for Tales for Sleepless Nights was “brought to life by a fresh team of upcoming actors and directors. Rather than jump scares, it builds a slow creeping dream perfect for horror.”

Another means through which Shimotsu (Best Wishes to All, Shudder’s New Group) finds the essence of Ito in all the episodes he helmed is through stillness in the performances and camerawork that evokes the comic book pages. He told a fan that he hopes to push fidelity to the material one step further in season 2 by shooting at least one episode in black-and-white, Ito’s preferred mode of illustration.

When asked by a con attendee which of Ito’s works he would most like to adapt next, the director earned applause by answering Uzumaki, the groundbreaking horror manga which has been brought to the screen several times, including a recent 4-part anime series for Adult Swim. The latter version had a famously rocky production, with quality diving after the first episode to the point that the fourth installment had no director credit. A new live-action version would be incredible—and incredibly strange—in Yûta Shimotsu’s hands.

“I would love to keep creating very bizarre, unique aesthetics like Mr. Ito's work. That's my goal,” said Shimotsu. “I'm developing a Hollywood project, so see you soon.”

entries.title: Kids’ Content Is Deeply Broken. A New Platform Wants to Fix It
entries.summary: Low-quality AI-generated content currently dominates children’s media. Maka, a streaming platform run by child development experts, is offering an alternative.
entries.content:
If you have young kids or if you know somebody who does, then you know about YouTube’s AI slop problem.

Videos targeted at children on the platform are often filled with bizarre and hyperstimulating content that’s AI generated. Not all of it is age-appropriate. These videos autoplay on endless, algorithmically curated streams punctuated by ads.

Maka, a new streaming app for kids aged 0 to 6, is positioning itself as an antidote to that concern. The platform has zero ads and doesn’t allow autoplay or endless scrolling, and its algorithms intentionally do not maximize watch time.

The company’s cofounder and chief product officer, Tanyella Leta, tells WIRED the platform is purposely abandoning the mechanisms that “turn children’s media into an engagement machine.”

Maka’s CEO and cofounder Isabel Sheinman adds that a lot of the streamers were built to serve adults, not children. “Kids were really the afterthought,” she says. Sheinman wants to set a much higher bar for what quality looks like in children’s media, which she says has been warped by harmful incentives. “Maka was built with child development science and children's behavior first and foremost.”

Launching today, Maka’s programming slate is a mix of licensed content from global studios and independent creators. It features 25 shows in its curated catalog, including Franklin, The Wiggles, Pocoyo, Vida the Vet, and Sesame Street. The platform runs on a subscription service, with a $15 monthly plan and a $107 annual plan.

It was during the Covid pandemic that Sheinman and Leta became obsessed with thinking about how to redesign kids' media. The solution? Every episode streamed on Maka is evaluated by child development experts through Imprint, a framework created with researchers at the Yale Child Study Center. The evaluation process, which examines everything from scene cuts to how fast-paced content is, maps child development across seven core domains. It looks for things like emotional regulation, kindness, how child-caregiver relationships are modeled in a story, and how a story might support critical thinking or language development.

AI-generated content has only added a new wrinkle to kids’ entertainment: videos are incoherent, have no plot, or contain outright misinformation but are packaged to look like learning. Some of it, as WIRED has previously reported, is disturbingly sexualized, featuring gore and other fetishes.

Michael Robb, head of research at the media literacy nonprofit Common Sense Media, says that on a platform like YouTube, slop videos that have the veneer of education sit side by side with carefully designed educational shows. Robb believes YouTube and other kids’ streaming platforms have not done enough to distinguish educational content from slop, which has only made filtering content harder for parents. “Platforms have taken steps to reduce kids’ exposure to age-inappropriate content, and that matters. But ‘not inappropriate’ is a very low bar. There’s a big gulf between that and media created intentionally with kids in mind.”

A 2020 study by Common Sense Media on YouTube videos watched by young kids found 75 percent had “weak or no educational value.” Kids also frequently ended up watching ads and content intended for older audiences.

According to its policy for YouTube Kids, which lets parents approve specific content themselves, YouTube excludes videos that are “deceptive, sensational, or clickbait” but acknowledges that not every video has been manually reviewed. YouTube also makes clear that automated filtering cannot guarantee every video will be appropriate. “There’s a chance that your child will find content that you don't want them to watch,” the company notes in its support docs.

Earlier this year, in an effort to encourage better digital literacy among kids, the American Academy of Pediatrics updated its guidance beyond screen time recommendations, urging children to avoid “AI-generated content,” “AI chatbots,” “short-form videos,” and “highly sensationalized content or clickbait.” The guide prioritized quality content and coviewing with parents rather than passive watching.

Tiffany Munzer, a developmental-behavioral pediatrician and digital media researcher at the University of Michigan, was the lead author on Academy of Pediatrics’s “Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents” policy statement, and tells WIRED in an email that the proliferation of low-quality content has led kids to “miss out on important, slower learning opportunities that promote critical thinking, generate new ideas, and practice stretching their attention spans.”

In April, child advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter, signed by more than 200 organizations and individual experts, asking YouTube to address the spread of AI videos on its platforms, saying AI slop “harms children’s development by distorting their sense of reality, overwhelming their learning processes and hijacking their attention.”

A YouTube spokesperson tells WIRED that on YouTube Kids, which is meant for kids 12 and under, AI content is limited to a small set of high-quality channels, and parents have the option to block channels entirely. The platform has stricter standards for content made for younger viewers, the company says.

For Maka’s business model to succeed, its shows will need to entertain and educate kids while also establishing confidence in parents. “The value that parents want is relief, knowing that what their child is seeing has been vetted by child development experts and everything on Maka they can trust is good for their kid,” Sheiman says.

Yalda Uhls, a former film executive at Sony and MGM who is now a researcher at UCLA focusing on how media affects the social learning of young children, worries that as AI revolutionizes kids’ streaming content, people who study child development are being left out of the process. “When I was a studio executive, every story meant for children passed through layers of accountable adults,” she says. “But today, algorithms, anonymous creators, and AI tools shape what kids see, and people who study child development are rarely in the room.”

“The gatekeepers have been replaced by a metric: minutes watched,” Uhls says. “Nobody in that chain is required to ask what a child is actually learning.”

One of Maka’s core features is a timer that parents set at the start of every viewing session to help the child wind down off the screen. As the show concludes, a character Maka developed named Scoot appears on the screen to get the child ready to detach from their device. Features like that are the difference between capturing a child’s attention versus earning it, Sheinman says. “So it becomes less of a moment of tension in a family and a moment that the child is prepared for.”

The founders ultimately want Maka to help change the perception of kids' relationship to screens.

“We’re seeing a really big challenge around the judgment of parents,” says Leta, explaining that one problem with screen time is the demonization of parents who rely on it. “We have all judged parents who bring out the screen on the train or at a restaurant. Let's be real, most parents will reach for the screen at some point. We don't think that they should be judged for that choice.”

Whether any of this will work is unclear. One question at the core of Maka’s mission is whether it can build a successful streaming company without adopting the same incentives that created the problems it is trying to solve.

Robb from Common Sense Media calls competing with YouTube a Herculean task. “YouTube is free and already on the devices within their homes. Moving them away can be tricky,” he says. The real test for Maka, Robb says, “will be whether it can grow with kids and stay sustainable without being pulled back toward the engagement metrics that drive the rest of the industry.”

Leta, one of Maka’s cofounders, admits that it’s easy to be cynical when it comes to children and screens. “But TV also gave us Sesame Street. It gave us Fred Rogers, who believed that the space between the child and the screen was sacred ground.”

“One of the dads in our beta told us that with other platforms, when his kid is watching, it feels like ‘a race to the bottom of my kid’s brainstem,’” Leta says. “It doesn't have to be like that.”

entries.title: Democrats Are Gearing Up to Investigate the Trump Administration. It Won’t Be Easy
entries.summary: As a recent government report on DOGE shows, even getting basic information out of the Trump administration will put a new Congress to the test.
entries.content:
As polls indicate Democrats could take back the US House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the Trump administration. But that may prove to be a difficult task, even with a majority in both chambers of Congress.

In late September, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) released a report on Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency titled “DOGE: Congress and the Public Lack Assurance That Systems and Data Were Protected at Multiple Agencies.” In it, the GAO revealed that multiple executive branch agencies had refused to fully cooperate with investigators about the extent and nature of DOGE’s access to sensitive systems and information. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), which DOGE and the Trump administration gutted in the early months of the president’s second term, sent the GAO a letter accusing investigators of bias and alleging the report was “misleading.”

The report, just the latest example of the Trump administration seeking to dodge congressional oversight, raises questions about what—if any—avenues the legislature has to enforce accountability, or even access basic information about what the government has been doing.

“In a world where there is no shame, it’s hard to think of what Congress can do that doesn’t involve some coercion of some kind,” says Emily Berman, a law professor at the University of Houston. “Like withholding money or going to court.”

The GAO serves as Congress’ primary investigative body; its work is most often initiated by requests from Congress but it is independent and nonpartisan. It does not, however, have the ability to enforce laws or take on prosecution. Federal agencies don’t necessarily have to enact the agency’s suggestions but they are legally required to cooperate with GAO’s requests for information and auditing.

The GAO and a Democratic congressional aide who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity, though, say that the agencies investigated by the GAO for the DOGE report—the CFPB, the Department of Veterans’ Affairs (VA), the Department of Education, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and the Small Business Administration (SBA)—all, in one way or another, refused to cooperate with the investigation.

“We have experienced increased challenges in obtaining information from agencies over the past year and a half,” GAO spokesperson Sarah Kaczmarek says. “As this report demonstrates, when agencies do not provide requested information, it can limit GAO’s ability to provide Congress and the public with assurance that federal programs, systems, and information are appropriately managed and protected.”

As an example, every agency included in the report refused to do so much as name which DOGE operatives they’d played host to—even when that information had already been publicly reported. The CFPB refused to name all six of the DOGE operatives who were detailed to the agency even though, in February 2025, WIRED identified three of them: Nikhil Rajpal, Chris Young, and Gavin Kliger. DOGE members Jeremy Lewin and Jordan Wick were also part of the team at the agency.
